extracted.intended_audience: OSHA rulewriters, employers, occupational health professionals, and public health researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Scientific and clinical standards and surveillance criteria for identifying, diagnosing, treating, documenting, and surveilling occupational heat-related illnesses and deaths, as presented in an OSHA proposed rule preamble. Includes diagnostic definitions, coding systems, physiological mechanisms, treatment timing, and return-to-work protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat strain and bodily responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The resulting bodily responses to occupational heat exposure are collectively referred to as heat strain (Cramer and Jay, 2016). These responses serve to decrease stored heat by increasing heat loss to the environment to maintain a stable body temperature (NIOSH, 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the brain recognizes stored heat it activates the autonomic nervous system: blood is shunted toward the skin (vasodilation) increasing blood flow near the skin surface, and sweat glands release water to wet the skin. These processes allow cooling by (1) radiation, (2) convection, (3) evaporation (as clothing/PPE permits), and (4) conduction (e.g., ice-containing vests). The extent of heat release depends on environmental conditions (air flow, temperature, relative humidity). High relative humidity reduces evaporation; retained sweat can cause heat rash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweat response consequences and electrolyte depletion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweating to cool the body can deplete the body's stores of water and electrolytes (e.g., sodium [Na], potassium [K], chloride [Cl], calcium [Ca], and magnesium [Mg]) that are essential for normal bodily function (Shirreffs and Maughan, 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electrolyte depletion can lead to hyponatremia and painful muscle spasms called heat cramps (Kamijo and Nose, 2006). Dehydration from fluid loss reduces circulating blood volume (Trangmar and Gonzalez-Alonso, 2017), contributing to heat illness progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological consequences of vasodilation and reduced circulating blood volume
rubrics_metrics.description: During vasodilation blood can pool in gravity-dependent areas and fluid can seep from blood vessels causing heat edema. Upright standing exacerbates pooling in the legs and lowers circulating blood volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large reductions in circulating blood volume can (1) cause continued rise in core body temperature and (2) reduce blood flow to brain, muscles, and organs, leading to neurological disturbances (heat stroke and syncope), extreme muscle fatigue and damage (heat exhaustion and rhabdomyolysis), and multi-organ damage (heart, liver, kidneys). Heat stroke and rhabdomyolysis can be fatal without prompt treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coding systems to identify heat-related illnesses (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical providers and public health professionals use coding systems to identify fatalities and non-fatal cases of various illnesses and injuries, including heat-related illnesses and injuries (HRIs). The medical and scientific communities use data from these coding systems to study incidence and prevalence of HRIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA relied on studies using these coding systems in its Health Effects and Risk Assessment sections. Coding systems standardize diagnosis recording and are used in surveillance systems; multiple codes may be recorded for a patient with multiple diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes for heat-related health effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICD System harmonizes diagnosis of disease; ICD codes correspond to highly specific medical diagnoses. The ICD system has multiple codes medical personnel can use when diagnosing HRIs (ICD-9 and ICD-10 used in cited studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table IV-1 maps ICD-9 to ICD-10 heat-related codes (examples: ICD-9 992 → ICD-10 T67; 992.0 heatstroke/sunstroke → T67.0; 992.1 heat syncope → T67.1, etc.). Codes shown exclude some related codes (e.g., X32 exposure to sunlight). Additional non-specific codes (e.g., M62.82 for rhabdomyolysis) may be used where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health surveillance systems leveraging ICD codes
rubrics_metrics.description: CDC and other systems leverage ICD-10 codes to collect data on heat-related deaths and HRIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CDC uses codes in the National Syndromic Surveillance System (NSSP) for near real-time data and in the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS) / National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for annual data. U.S. Armed Forces use ICD-10 codes in the Defense Medical Surveillance System (DMSS) and the Army's Total Army Injury and Health Outcomes Database (TAIHOD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational Illness and Injury Classification System (OIICS) codes for heat-related effects
rubrics_metrics.description: BLS developed the OIICS to harmonize reporting of injuries and illnesses affecting U.S. workers; each code specifies a diagnosis (nature code) and event(s) leading to it (event code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIICS has multiple codes for occupational HRIs (Version 3.0 is current). Table IV-2 lists nature codes (e.g., 172 effects of heat and light; 1721 heat stroke, syncope; 1722 heat exhaustion, fatigue; 2893 prickly heat/heat rash) and event codes (e.g., 53 exposure to temperature extremes; 5311 exposure to environmental heat—indoor; 5312 outdoor). BLS applies OIICS to CFOI and SOII data; older versions were used in some data but major categories did not change significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of surveillance and coding: underreporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation to relying on coding systems to identify heat-related fatalities and HRIs is underreporting; numerous studies indicate HRIs are likely vastly underreported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include underreporting by workers to employers, underreporting by employers to BLS and OSHA, underutilization of workers' compensation, structural and cultural factors affecting help-seeking, and difficulties determining heat-related causes of death. Therefore coding-system-derived statistics likely underestimate true burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-related death mechanisms and affected organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mora et al. (2017) identified five harmful physiological mechanisms triggered by heat exposure that can lead to death: ischemia, heat cytotoxicity, inflammatory response, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and rhabdomyolysis. They also identified seven vital organs commonly critically impacted: brain, heart, kidneys, lungs, pancreas, intestines, and liver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Across these mechanisms and organs, 27 pathways were identified whereby heat exposure could lead to organ failure and fatality. Heat stroke is the most common cause of occupational heat-related deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat as underlying cause vs significant contributing condition (ICD guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: ICD-10 defines underlying cause as the disease or injury which initiated the train of morbid events leading directly to death, or circumstances producing the fatal injury. A significant contributing condition is one that contributed to the fatal outcome but was not related to the disease directly causing death (WHO, 2016; WHO, 2004).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthcare professionals should document heat in the appropriate field (underlying cause or contributing condition) when supported by clinical/investigative information.

rubrics_metrics.name: NAME definition and criteria for heat-related death
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME) defines 'heat-related death' as 'a death in which exposure to high ambient temperature either caused the death or significantly contributed to it' (Donoghue et al., 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to NAME, cause is ascertained based on circumstances (e.g., known heat wave), investigative reports, or a pre-death temperature ≥105 °F. Heat may be designated a significant contributing condition if antemortem body temperature cannot be established but environmental temperature at collapse was high, or if heat exacerbated a pre-existing disease. Autopsy findings are often nonspecific; diagnosis is principally based on investigative information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of work-related heat deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes exist to identify and document deaths that are work-related: death certificates include a field for 'injury at work' and work-related fatalities are identified through CFOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFOI is a cooperative federal-state program that uses administrative records (including death certificates) to produce counts of fatal work injuries; it examines cases marked 'At work' to ascertain cause(s) of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat stroke definition (NIOSH) and hallmark characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH defines heat stroke as 'an acute medical emergency caused by exposure to heat from an excessive rise in body temperature [above 41.1 °C (106 °F)] and failure of the [body's] temperature-regulating mechanism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hallmarks of heat stroke are (1) central nervous system dysfunction (encephalopathy manifesting as irrational behavior, confusion, coma, convulsions) and (2) damage to multiple organs (kidneys, liver, heart, pancreas, GI tract, circulatory system). Heat stroke is life-threatening and requires urgent treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of heat stroke: classic and exertional
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types: classic heat stroke (CHS) and exertional heat stroke (EHS). CHS can occur without activity and is associated with high ambient temperature and humidity (heat waves), often affecting children and elderly. EHS occurs as a result of physical activity and can affect healthy individuals regardless of environmental heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EHS can occur with any amount of physical exertion, even within first 60 minutes. Diagnosis can be recorded via ICD codes; medical examiners may note heat stroke on death certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological mechanisms of heat stroke (three mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three accepted mechanisms through which heat exposure can cause CNS dysfunction and/or multi-organ damage: (1) reduced cerebral blood velocity leading to orthostatic intolerance and reduced cerebral perfusion; (2) vascular endothelium damage leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with microclots and bleeding causing organ injury; (3) gut epithelium damage causing endotoxemia and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mechanisms share origin in excessive heat stress/hyperthermia and explain CNS dysfunction and multi-organ damage; liver often among first organs damaged and can precipitate heat stroke death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational heat stroke epidemiology and severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupational heat stroke occurs across industries and settings; studies report high hospitalization rates and mortality. Example: in a Florida hospital study during warm seasons (2005-2012) heat stroke was primary diagnosis in 91% of deaths among work-related HRIs; among military EHS patients ~73% required hospitalization for at least two days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BLS CFOI identified 1,042 U.S. worker deaths due to heat exposure (1992–2022) but underreporting may mean true numbers are higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment timing and cooling targets for heat stroke
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat stroke treatment requires immediate rest, cooling, and usually hospitalization. Prognosis depends on prompt recognition and rapid cooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For EHS, cooling the body below 104 °F within 30 minutes of collapse is associated with very good outcomes; rapid cooling within one hour for CHS reduced mortality from 33% to 15% in one study. Delays in cooling increase risk of tissue damage, multi-organ dysfunction, and death. Some individuals are resistant to rapid cooling, and outcomes vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return-to-work and recovery protocols after heat stroke
rubrics_metrics.description: Recovery may require time away from work; return-to-duty protocols vary by setting and use laboratory normalization and graded functional capacity assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military protocols assign grades for functional capacity and restrict maximal exertion until labs normalize and tolerance demonstrated; typical trial periods include up to three months with restrictions. U.S. Navy delays full return to duty 2 days to 3 weeks. ACSM (2023) recommends at least 7 days rest after EHS, then gradual re-acclimatization over 2–4 weeks with full return 2–4 weeks after demonstrating tolerance; if not back to pre-EHS levels in 4–6 weeks, further evaluation. NATA recommends 7–21 days rest, asymptomatic status, normal labs, and physician clearance before gradual return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term effects and subsequent health risks after exertional heat illness/heat stroke
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited studies indicate long-term effects: prior EHS associated with higher prevalence of acute ischemic stroke, acute myocardial infarction, and nearly three-fold higher prevalence of chronic kidney disease; animal studies suggest epigenetic effects causing immunosuppression and metabolic disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 10–20% of people who had heat stroke experience heat intolerance ~2 months after; some cases of prolonged heat intolerance (months to years) have been reported, increasing risk for subsequent heat stroke. These potential long-term risks support cautious return-to-work and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion definition and diagnostic considerations (NIOSH)
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH defines heat exhaustion as '[a] heat-related illness characterized by elevation of core body temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F) and abnormal performance of one or more organ systems, without injury to the central nervous system.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include profuse sweating, changes in mental status, dizziness, nausea, headache, irritability, weakness, decreased urine output, and elevated core temperature up to 40 °C (104 °F). Heat exhaustion may progress to heat stroke; clinical differentiation between heat exhaustion and early heat stroke can be difficult. Armstrong et al. (2007) recommend rectal temperature to distinguish between the two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological mechanisms of heat exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat exhaustion occurs when heat stress results in elevated body temperature between 37 °C and 40 °C (98.6 °F and 104 °F) with physiological changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these conditions, heavy sweating occurs, tissue perfusion is reduced, inflammatory mediators are released, and electrolyte imbalances can result from sweat losses and inadequate replenishment. 'Voluntary dehydration' (not rehydrating despite availability) can exacerbate the condition.
